lesson_title: The Four Sociological Perspectives

findings.claim: Walby identified six structures of patriarchy: paid employment, household production, culture, sexuality, violence and the state
findings.notes: The first structure is named 'paid employment' here, but Walby's actual terminology in Theorizing Patriarchy (1990) is 'paid work'. The second is 'household production' but Walby uses 'housework' in her direct statement. Both are common variations in secondary sources and do not misrepresent the theory, but 'paid work' is the accurate term. A student memorising from this lesson would write 'paid employment', which differs from the L07 Walby lesson (which correctly says 'paid work'). Minor inconsistency.

lesson_title: Divorce: Causes, Consequences and Theoretical Perspectives

findings.claim: In the decade after the Second World War, divorce was relatively rare — around 25,000 divorces per year in England and Wales
findings.notes: ONS historical data shows approximately 25,000–35,000 divorces per year in England and Wales in the late 1940s–early 1950s. 'Around 25,000' is a reasonable estimate for the immediate post-war period.

findings.claim: By the mid-1990s this had risen to around 175,000 per year
findings.notes: The actual ONS peak was 165,018 divorces in 1993, not 175,000. The peak year was 1993, not 'mid-1990s' (which implies 1994–1996). The figure is overstated by approximately 6% and the timing is off. Not a fabrication but a notable inaccuracy in a specific statistic.

findings.claim: The Divorce Reform Act 1969, which came into force in 1971, fundamentally changed the legal basis of divorce in England and Wales
findings.notes: Royal Assent October 1969, commenced 1 January 1971. Confirmed.

findings.claim: The Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 (which came into force in April 2022) introduced no-fault divorce
findings.notes: Act passed June 2020, came into force 6 April 2022. Confirmed.

lesson_title: Processes Inside Schools

findings.claim: Hargreaves's study Deviance in Classrooms (1975) examined how teachers label pupils as 'deviant' within school settings
findings.notes: Deviance in Classrooms by Hargreaves, Hester and Mellor (1975) confirmed. The lesson names only Hargreaves as author — minor simplification of a co-authored work, but standard in GCSE contexts.

findings.claim: Becker (Outsiders, 1963) introduced the concept of master status: a label that overrides all other aspects of a person's identity
findings.notes: Becker did not originate 'master status' — the concept was coined by Everett Hughes in a 1945 article 'Dilemmas and Contradictions of Status' (American Journal of Sociology). Becker adopted and popularised the term in Outsiders (1963). Attributing the concept's introduction to Becker is a misattribution of origin, though standard in many GCSE resources. Students writing that Becker 'introduced' master status would be technically incorrect.

findings.notes: Year 1977, 12 boys, West Midlands location all confirmed. Willis pseudonymously called the location 'Hammertown' for anonymity; the school is described as being in the West Midlands / Midlands.

lesson_title: Walby on Patriarchy and Power Relationships

findings.claim: Sylvia Walby (1990) provided the most comprehensive sociological account of patriarchy in her work Theorizing Patriarchy
findings.notes: Publication year 1990 confirmed.

findings.claim: Walby's Theorizing Patriarchy (1990) identified six structures through which patriarchy operates: paid work, household production, patriarchal culture, sexuality, male violence, and the state
findings.notes: The lesson consistently uses 'household production' where Walby's direct text uses 'housework', and adds qualifiers ('patriarchal' culture, 'male' violence) not in Walby's own list. These are consistent with many secondary sources but diverge from Walby's own wording: 'paid work, housework, culture, sexuality, violence and the state.' LOW issue — not a fabrication, but a terminological variation worth noting for students who may look up the original.

The lesson's citation '(1938, enlarged 1968)' is a sensible compression — it correctly identifies the original article date and the enlarged edition. This is acceptable.

lesson_title: Marxist, Interactionist and Feminist Theories of Crime

findings.claim: William Chambliss, in his landmark study Saints and Roughnecks (1973), provided one of the most vivid demonstrations of how social class shapes the application of the law. Chambliss observed two groups of adolescent boys in a small American town over two years. The 'Saints' were eight middle-class boys who regularly truanted, drank and engaged in petty crime. The 'Roughnecks' were six working-class boys
findings.notes: Chambliss (1973) Saints and Roughnecks confirmed. Eight Saints and six Roughnecks confirmed. Publication year confirmed.
